intro:
These exercises drill the four decisions that make associative collections behave well in production: which of HashMap, HashSet, BTreeMap, or BTreeSet matches the contract; how to read across the table boundary without allocating a key; how to express read-modify-write as a single Entry path; and how to make output deterministic on purpose rather than by accident. Each one applies the ownership instincts from earlier chapters to hashed and ordered storage.

The through-line is that a hash map has exactly one inbound move (insert) and a borrow-only read path. Once you see the API split along that line, the rest follows: borrow on reads, own only when you store, and treat iteration order as something you choose at the boundary, not something the hash table promises.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose map, set, or tree from the contract
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Decide each case from its semantics, not from which type you reach for most often. The chapter frames this as two yes-or-no questions: do you need a value per key or only membership (map versus set), and does anything downstream depend on iteration order (hashed versus ordered)?

Request counter keyed by route: this is genuine key-value association. The route is the key, the count is the value, and nothing in the contract requires a particular iteration order. Choose HashMap<String, usize> for expected fast lookup and update.

Dedup list of active feature flags: the value is really 'present or absent.' There is no per-key payload, only membership and deduplication. Choose HashSet<String>. Using HashMap<String, bool> here would be a boolean map standing in for a set, which is exactly the improvised shape the chapter warns against.

Config renderer that must emit stable sorted output: here deterministic iteration order is part of the external contract, because operators and snapshot tests read the output. Choose BTreeMap so the ordering is the data structure's job rather than something you re-sort at every render. (If the keys carried no values you would pick BTreeSet instead.)

Ordered allow-list supporting range-like prefix reviews: this is about ordering, not lookup speed. Range and prefix scans need keys kept in sorted order, which a hash table cannot provide. Choose BTreeSet (or BTreeMap if each entry needs a value). The justification is operational: the workload asks for ordered traversal and ranges, and only the tree variants offer that.
criteria: HashMap<String, usize> chosen for the unordered route counter (key-value association, order not contractual).
HashSet<String> chosen for active flags, since the workload is membership and deduplication only.
BTreeMap chosen for the config renderer because stable sorted output is part of the boundary contract.
Each choice is justified operationally (lookup vs membership vs ordered/range traversal), not by naming the type alone.

exerciseSolutions.title: Remove duplicate lookups with Entry API
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The inherited shape does contains_key, then get_mut, then insert on the same key. Conceptually that is three trips into the table for one logical update: contains_key hashes the key and probes a bucket, get_mut hashes and probes again, and insert hashes and probes a third time. The duplicate work is the repeated hashing and bucket lookup for a single key path. It is also a correctness hazard, because the presence check and the mutation are separate statements that can drift apart during maintenance.

The Entry API collapses this into one path. You call entry(key) once, which does a single probe and hands back a view of the slot whether or not it was occupied. From there you choose the helper that matches the intent. For a counter, or_insert(0) gives you a mutable reference to the slot (creating it at 0 if absent), and you add one in place. or_default() does the same when the value type's Default is what you want as the initial state. and_modify(...).or_insert(...) is the right shape when the present case and the absent case need different logic, for example incrementing an existing counter but seeding a freshly created one differently. For a plain increment, or_insert is the cleanest fit.

The owned-versus-borrowed distinction matters because entry takes the key by value. If the caller already owns the key (a parsed String), entry(key) simply moves it in at no extra cost. If the caller only borrows &str, you must produce an owned key to insert, so entry(route.to_owned()) allocates a String even though the read path could have borrowed. Entry removes the duplicate lookups; it does not remove that allocation. Borrowed lookup (get/contains by &str) is the separate fast path for reads that never need to store anything.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Entry replaces contains_key + get_mut + insert with a single probe and an in-place update.
criteria: Explains that the original repeats key hashing and bucket probing three times for one update.
Selects or_insert for the plain counter and explains where or_default and and_modify fit instead.
States that entry takes the key by value: owned keys move in for free, while a borrowed &str forces an owning allocation to store.

exerciseSolutions.title: Implement borrowed lookup for owned string keys
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Both helpers read across the table boundary, so they should borrow and never allocate. A HashMap<String, usize> can be queried with a &str directly, and a HashSet<String> can test membership with a &str directly. This works because the lookup methods are generic over a borrowed form of the key: String borrows as str, and str's equality and hashing match what String would produce, so the borrowed query lands in the same bucket as the stored owned key.

The defect to avoid is get(&route.to_string()) or contains(&route.to_string()), which allocates a throwaway String on every read just to immediately discard it. Pass route straight through: get(route) and contains(route). The parameter stays &str, and nothing is allocated on the read path.

The return types stay small and owned even though the lookup borrows. route_count copies the usize out with copied() and defaults to 0 when absent, returning a plain value rather than a borrowed &usize tied to the map's lifetime. is_active returns a bool. Neither helper hands back a reference into the collection, so callers are not constrained by the map's borrow.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Query owned String keys by borrowed &str; copy small values out instead of borrowing them.
criteria: The lookup parameter stays &str in both helpers.
Uses borrowed lookup get(route) and contains(route) directly on the owned-key collections.
No throwaway String is allocated on the read path; results are returned as an owned usize/bool, not a borrowed reference.

exerciseSolutions.title: Make output deterministic on purpose
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is treating HashMap iteration order as stable. The default hasher uses randomized state per process, so iterating a HashMap yields entries in an order that can differ across runs. A snapshot test that iterates the map directly therefore flaps not because the data changed but because the render path inherited a non-deterministic order it was never promised.

There are two principled fixes, and which one is correct depends on how widely order is needed. If only the output edge cares about order, keep the hot mutable index as a HashMap and sort or project at the render boundary: collect into a BTreeMap (or sort a Vec of pairs) just before formatting. This keeps fast unordered updates on the write path and pays the ordering cost once, only when emitting. If every caller wants stable order anyway, stop projecting repeatedly and make BTreeMap the primary representation, so ordering is the storage contract rather than a step you must remember at each output site.

The tradeoff is explicit. Sorting at the boundary keeps amortized expected O(1) updates and adds an O(n log n) sort (or O(n log n) BTreeMap build) per render; it is the right call when output is occasional and updates are hot. Making BTreeMap primary gives you ordered iteration everywhere for free but changes update and lookup cost to O(log n) and removes the unordered fast path. Either is defensible; choosing one deliberately is the point. The fix is not 'sort until the test passes' but 'state where the order contract lives and honor it consistently.'
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Project the HashMap into a BTreeMap at the render edge, or make BTreeMap primary if order is always required.
criteria: Identifies that the bug is relying on randomized HashMap iteration order as if it were stable.
Proposes both options: sort/project at the boundary, or use BTreeMap as the primary representation when order is always needed.
Justifies the tradeoff (hot unordered updates plus per-render sort vs uniformly ordered O(log n) storage) in contract terms, not just making the test green.

exerciseSolutions.title: Separate owned update paths from borrowed read paths
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The teammate's counts.entry(route.to_string()).or_insert(0) is correct and it does optimize something real, but it is not free, and the review should say all three things precisely.

What Entry removes: duplicate table lookups on the update path. Without Entry, a presence check followed by a mutate followed by an insert hashes and probes the same key two or three times. entry probes once and returns a handle to the slot, so the read-modify-write becomes a single trip into the table. That is a genuine win and the main reason to reach for Entry.

What still costs: route is a borrowed &str, and entry takes the key by value, so route.to_string() allocates a fresh owned String on every call even when the entry already exists and the allocated key is immediately dropped. Entry eliminated the duplicate lookups; it did nothing about the allocation. 'Fewer lookups' is not 'zero allocation,' and conflating the two is the slogan to avoid.

When this is the right design: most of the time. If routes come from a bounded, low-cardinality set, if the counter update is not the measured hot path, or if you genuinely need to insert new owned keys anyway, the per-call allocation is noise and the clarity of one Entry path wins. When to revisit: if this update sits on a profiled hot path with high call volume and a key space that is mostly already-present (so nearly every to_string allocates only to be discarded), the allocation can dominate. Then you separate the two fast paths: try a borrowed read first (get_mut(route) to bump an existing counter without allocating) and only fall back to an owning insert when the key is actually new, allocating the key exactly once over its lifetime.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Entry removes duplicate probes; the owning to_string remains. Split paths only when profiling shows it matters.
criteria: Explains that Entry removes the duplicate table lookups on the read-modify-write path.
States explicitly that route.to_string() still allocates an owned String key on every call, even on the already-present path.
Gives an acceptable case (cold/clear path, keys often new) and a revisit case (profiled hot path with mostly-present keys where the discarded allocation dominates).

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose a hasher and threat model deliberately
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Hasher choice is partly a security decision and partly a performance decision, and the two systems sit on opposite sides of that line. The default standard-library hasher uses randomized per-process state, which makes worst-case collision behavior unpredictable to an outsider. That randomization is a deliberate defense: it is why the default is the right choice on attacker-controlled inputs.

The internet-facing API gateway is keyed by client-controlled strings, so collision behavior is part of its threat model. An attacker who can predict which keys collide can force a HashMap toward worst-case probing and turn lookups into a denial-of-service vector (a hash-flooding attack). Keep this path conservative: stay on the randomized default unless there is an exceptionally strong, measured reason to change, and never adopt a fast non-randomized hasher here just because it benchmarked well internally. A faster internal benchmark does not address the public threat model.

The internal analytics worker is keyed by trusted numeric IDs on a path you control and can measure. It is the legitimate candidate for experimentation with a faster non-randomized or domain-specific hasher, because the inputs are not adversarial and the keys are small and frequent. But that is an engineering decision, not a reflex: benchmark first, change second.

Before approving any hasher change I would require production signals, not micro-benchmarks alone: a CPU profile showing hashing is actually a hot cost, an allocation profile, p99/p999 latency under representative load, and evidence about collision-sensitive behavior for the real key distribution. The code-review note must document the trust boundary explicitly: state that the inputs on this path are trusted and non-adversarial, why the alternative hasher was chosen, what was measured, and an instruction that this hasher must not be copied onto any externally reachable, attacker-influenced path. If the trust boundary later moves (the internal worker starts ingesting external keys), the hasher decision has to be revisited.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Default randomized hasher on the public boundary; a measured non-randomized hasher only behind a documented trust note internally.
criteria: Keeps the attacker-controlled gateway path on the conservative randomized default absent a very strong reason.
Treats the trusted internal worker as a measurement candidate rather than an automatic change.
Names concrete production signals (CPU profile, allocation profile, p99 latency, collision-sensitive behavior) required before approval.
Documents the trust boundary and tradeoff, including a warning not to reuse the hasher on externally reachable paths.

labSolution.explanation:
The lab repairs three separate anti-patterns from the initial code, one per helper, each illustrating a core idea from the chapter.

record_owned replaces the contains_key / index / insert sequence with a single Entry path. entry(route) moves the owned key into the table and probes the bucket once; or_insert(0) creates the slot at zero if it is absent and otherwise leaves it, returning a mutable reference; *slot += 1 mutates in place. Calling it for "api", "billing", then "api" again leaves api at 2 and billing at 1. lookup fixes the wasteful get(&route.to_string()), which allocated a throwaway String per read, with get(route) querying the owned String keys directly by borrowed &str, then copied() to return an owned Option<usize>. So lookup(&counts, "api") yields Some(2), printed as 'api = Some(2)'.

render_sorted fixes the determinism bug: iterating the HashMap directly exposed randomized hash order. Collecting the borrowed entries into a BTreeMap orders them by key, so formatting yields 'api=2,billing=1' deterministically every run. Together the two println! lines produce exactly the expected output. The program was compiled with rustc --edition 2021 -O and its stdout matched the expected output.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is `get("key")` on a `HashMap<String, V>` often better than `get(&"key".to_string())`?
reviewAnswers.answer: get accepts a borrowed form of the key, and String borrows as str with matching equality and hashing, so get("key") looks up the entry without allocating anything. get(&"key".to_string()) builds a fresh owned String purely to read, then drops it immediately, which is a wasted heap allocation on the read path. On a hot lookup path that allocation is pure overhead, so the borrowed query is both clearer and cheaper.

reviewAnswers.question: What does the Entry API optimize, and what does it not magically optimize away?
reviewAnswers.answer: Entry optimizes the read-modify-write path by collapsing a presence check, a mutable get, and an insert into a single table probe that returns a view of the slot, eliminating duplicate hashing and bucket lookups. What it does not remove is allocation of the key itself: entry takes the key by value, so if you only hold a borrowed &str, entry(route.to_owned()) still allocates an owned String even when the entry already exists. Fewer lookups is not the same as zero allocation, so on a hot, mostly-present path you may still split into a borrowed get_mut plus an owning insert only on first sight.

reviewAnswers.question: When is a `HashSet<T>` clearer than `HashMap<T, bool>`?
reviewAnswers.answer: Use HashSet<T> whenever the question is purely 'is this element present?', which is to say membership and deduplication with no per-key payload. HashMap<T, bool> can encode the same thing, but it invites a meaningless second state (a key mapped to false) and reads as if a real value matters when it does not. The set expresses intent directly with contains, insert, and the set-algebra operations, and removes the boolean-map ambiguity entirely.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is `HashMap` iteration order the wrong thing to rely on for stable output?
reviewAnswers.answer: The default hasher seeds randomized per-process state, so iteration order can differ between runs and is never promised to be stable. Any operator dump, log line, snapshot test, or downstream consumer that depends on that order will flap intermittently for reasons unrelated to the data. If order is part of the contract, make it explicit: sort or project at the render boundary, or use a BTreeMap so ordered iteration is the storage guarantee rather than an accident.

reviewAnswers.question: What extra question appears the moment you consider a custom hasher on a public boundary?
reviewAnswers.answer: You must ask whether collision behavior is part of your threat model, because on an attacker-controlled boundary it is. The randomized default hasher resists hash-flooding, where an adversary crafts colliding keys to force worst-case probing and cause a denial of service; a faster non-randomized hasher can throw that protection away. So a public-path hasher change is a security decision first and a performance decision second, and it needs a documented trust boundary plus production evidence, not just a faster internal benchmark.
